intro: Searching for a depression counsellor near you usually means you want someone local who understands how low mood can make everyday life feel heavy and hard to shift. You may be looking for yourself or for someone you care about, and you want to know who is nearby and how to take the first step. We introduce people to counsellors who work with depression, so you can speak to a professional and see whether it feels like the right fit.
need_heading: What people searching for a local depression counsellor often need
need_lead: Most people who type this search want a counsellor they can reach without a long journey, who can offer steady support for depression.
needs: You may be feeling persistently low, tearful or numb, and you want to talk to someone nearby who understands depression rather than having to travel far.
You might find it hard to leave the house some days, so a counsellor within easy reach makes it more likely you will keep going to regular sessions.
You could be worried about a friend or family member and want to find a local counsellor they can get to without too much effort.
You may have tried other things and now want a structured, talking approach close to home to help lift your mood.
You might want to combine counselling with lifestyle changes such as sleep, movement or routine, and a local counsellor can fit around that.
context_heading: What to know about choosing a counsellor for depression
context: "Counsellor" and "psychotherapist" are not protected titles in the UK, so anyone can use them. To protect yourself, look for a practitioner on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, such as BACP, UKCP or NCPS. Practitioner psychologists, who use titles such as clinical or counselling psychologist, must be registered with the HCPC.

Accredited registers require training, supervision, a code of ethics and a complaints procedure. A good therapist will explain their approach, confidentiality and its limits in the first session, so you know what to expect.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Mention that you are looking for a depression counsellor near you, and give your town or the area you can easily travel to.
Describe how depression is affecting you day to day, such as low mood, loss of interest, sleep or appetite changes, so we can introduce you to someone who works with these experiences.
Say whether you are looking for yourself or for someone else, and whether the person is an adult or a young person.
Explain any preference for how you would like to meet, such as in person locally, by phone or online, if that matters to you.
Let us know if you have had counselling before or if there is anything you found helpful or unhelpful about it.
Include any questions you want answered first, such as how sessions are structured or what happens if things get worse.
questions_heading: Questions to ask a depression counsellor
questions: How do you usually work with depression, and what approach do you use?
What happens in a first session, and how will you explain confidentiality and its limits?
Are you on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, such as BACP, UKCP or NCPS?
How often would we meet, and how do you decide when to look at how things are going?
What should I do if I feel worse between sessions or if things get worse?
Do you offer sessions locally in person, and is there anything I should arrange before the first meeting?

faqs.q: How do I find a depression counsellor near me?
faqs.a: Tell iComply your area and what you need, and we will introduce you to a counsellor who works with depression and is local to you. You then speak to them directly and they quote you for their service.

faqs.q: What should I look for in a counsellor for depression?
faqs.a: Look for someone on a register accredited by the Professional Standards Authority, such as BACP, UKCP or NCPS, and ask how they work with depression. A good counsellor will explain their approach and confidentiality in the first session.

faqs.q: Can counselling help if I also want to make lifestyle changes?
faqs.a: Yes, counselling can be combined with lifestyle support such as looking at sleep, routine and gentle movement. A counsellor can help you think about what else might support your mood alongside regular sessions.

faqs.q: What if I am feeling worse or having thoughts of harming myself?
faqs.a: Tell your counsellor if things get worse, and do not wait for your next session if you feel unsafe. You can contact NHS 111 for urgent advice or call 999 in an emergency.
